questions.question_text: A 70-year-old woman is referred by her general practitioner (GP) to you for psychiatric assessment. She mistakes her husband for her deceased father and later for her elder brother. She believes that she has never married. She also mistakes her daughter for her younger sister. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation:
Intermetamorphosis syndrome is a misidentification syndrome and the patient develops the delusional conviction that various people have been transformed physically and psychologically into other people.
Reference and Further Reading: Campbell RJ (1996). Psychiatric Dictionary. Oxford, UK: Oxford University Press.

questions.question_text: The community mental health team visits a 40-year-old man who describes the experience of being able to hear conversations from the police station in the neighbouring town. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation:
Extracampine hallucinations are hallucinations that occur beyond the limits of the sensory field. In this case, ‘hearing’ conversations from the neighbouring town is an auditory extracampine hallucination. Autoscopy is a visual hallucination of seeing a ‘double’ image of oneself viewed from within one’s physical body. The Doppelgänger phenomenon is the subjective feeling of doubling, where the person feels like his exact ‘double’ is present both outside alongside and inside oneself. Options (D) and (E) involve hallucinations that occur when one is falling asleep and waking up from sleep respectively.
Reference and Further Reading: Sims A (2003). Symptoms of the Mind: An Introduction to Descriptive Psychopathology. London: Saunders, pp. 105–106, 112, 217–220.

questions.question_text: When the conditioned response seems more prominent after multiple exposure to the original conditioned stimulus, it is typically known as
questions.explanation:
Incubation refers to the increase in strength of the conditioned response, resulting from multiple repeated brief exposures to the conditioned stimulus. Generalization refers to the process whereby a CR established to one stimulus is evoked by other similar stimuli. Discrimination is the differential recognition of similar stimuli.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 26.

questions.question_text: Based on your understanding of pharmacology, neuroleptic malignant syndrome is classified under which of the following particular type of side effect?
questions.explanation:
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome has been classified as an idiosyncratic reaction to medication. Idiosyncratic reactions are unpredictable adverse drug reactions associated with individual human differences.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 252.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the neurodevelopment and the neurochemistry of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is incorrect?

options.text: September is considered to be the peak month for births of children with ADHD and without comorbid learning disorders.
Early infection, inflammation, toxins and trauma would cause circulatory, metabolic and physical brain damage, which might lead to ADHD in adulthood.
Psychosocial adversity is not one of the key factors associated with ADHD in childhood.
A dysfunction in noradrenaline might lead to negative feedback to the locus coeruleus.
A dysfunction in noradrenaline might lead to a reduction of noradrenaline in the central nervous system (CNS).

correct_answer.text: Psychosocial adversity is not one of the key factors associated with ADHD in childhood.

correct_answers.text: Psychosocial adversity is not one of the key factors associated with ADHD in childhood.

questions.explanation:
Psychosocial adversity is one of the factors associated with ADHD in childhood. This includes maternal psychopathology, large family sizes, parental conflict and emotional deprivation.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 631.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old man is suspected to be a malingerer who tries to avoid court hearing and admitted himself to an orthopaedic ward for sudden paralysis. You want to examine his gait. Which of the following features strongly suggest that this man is indeed a malingerer?

options.text: Bending forward and advancing with rapid shuffling gait
Unable to commence gait during examination

correct_answer.text: Unable to commence gait during examination

correct_answers.text: Unable to commence gait during examination

questions.explanation:
A malingerer is unable to commence gait during examination when being watched. Option (A) refers to festinant gait in Parkinson’s disease. Option (B) is found in hysteria. Option (C) is found in Huntington’s disease.
Reference and Further Reading: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 682, 684.

questions.question_text: In this form of dysphasia, there are difficulties with comprehension. Which form of dysphasia would this be?
questions.explanation:
This is an example of receptive dysphasia. It usually involves damage to Wernicke’s area, disrupting comprehension of language. Speech rhythm and intonation are normal, but content is abnormal.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 105.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male suffered from a stroke recently, and after treatment, he is left with some speech difficulties. He is able to comprehend and understand what others are saying, but he is not able to formulate and say a sentence such that others would understand. Which form of dysphasia would this be?
questions.explanation:
This is expressive dysphasia due to damage in Broca’s area. Comprehension is intact, but speech production—rhythm, intonation, and grammar—is disrupted.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 105.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man with a history of cocaine misuse feels bugs on his skin. He scratches at the ‘bugs’ trying to remove them, gouging his skin and leaving scars. The psychopathology being described is
questions.explanation:
Formication is the sensation of insects crawling under the skin—a type of haptic (tactile) hallucination. Visceral hallucination is a deep sensation involving inner organs without a real stimulus.
Reference and Further Reading: Puri BK, Hall AD (2002). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: Arnold, p. 154.

questions.question_text: The concept of systematic desensitization that is being used in the treatment of anxiety-related disorders is based on which of the following behavioural models?
questions.explanation:
Systematic desensitization is based on reciprocal inhibition: relaxation reduces anxiety, and the two cannot coexist. Patients build an anxiety hierarchy and pair each step with relaxation.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 28.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old male has had a history of bipolar disorder and he has been on lithium monotherapy. He just returned from a trip to Singapore, where he did a lot of outdoor activities in the sun. He just also developed diarrhoea. Currently, he noticed that he has hand tremors. Which of the following side effect is he suffering from?
questions.explanation:
He has developed lithium toxicity, precipitated by dehydration (sun exposure, diarrhoea). Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and requires plasma level monitoring.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 254.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not considered to be a core symptom of adult ADHD?
questions.explanation:
In adult ADHD, inattentive symptoms predominate. Hyperactivity typically improves with age and is not a core adult symptom.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 631.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man has been diagnosed with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). He is concerned about getting other infections. Which opportunistic infection is the commonest life-threatening opportunistic infection seen in patients with AIDS?
questions.explanation:
Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (now Pneumocystis jirovecii) is the most common life-threatening opportunistic infection in AIDS.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, p. 789.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man has just suffered from an acute stroke. Immediately after the stroke, he realized that he is unable to understand written materials. However, when his care-giver spells the words out loud, he can immediately recognize them. He is still able to write. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Alexia without agraphia: lesion of the splenium of the corpus callosum prevents visual words from reaching the language areas, so he cannot read but can write. He learns compensation by naming letters aloud.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 107.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most characteristic and consistent abnormality in delirium?
questions.explanation:
Disturbance in attention (reduced ability to focus, shift or sustain attention) is the hallmark of delirium.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 511–513.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most lethal combination of medications in causing serotonin syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Phenelzine (MAOI) plus meperidine (opioid) has caused fatal serotonin syndrome repeatedly. Meperidine’s serotonergic action makes this particularly dangerous.
Reference: Sharav VH (2007). Serotonin syndrome: A mix of medicines that can be lethal. The New York Times.

questions.question_text: The local dual addictions services just introduced a new programme aimed at promoting cocaine abstinence. The new programme would last for 12 weeks, and for the initial 6 weeks, the participants would earn cash vouchers if their urine sample showed a 25% decrease in the amount of cocaine, and in the next 6 weeks, they would continue to earn cash vouchers if their urine sample was entirely negative. This method of promoting cocaine abstinence is based on which of the following psychological theories?
questions.explanation:
Shaping: successive approximations toward the target behaviour are reinforced (first 25% reduction, then complete abstinence).
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 29.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man, Peter, is referred by his GP to you for auditory hallucinations before he falls asleep. Which of the following is the most common presentation of such psychopathology?

options.text: Seeing a view of wide area

questions.explanation:
Hypnagogic hallucinations commonly involve hearing one’s own name called (e.g. “Peter, Peter”). These occur on falling asleep and may be normal.
Reference: Sims A (2003). Symptoms of the Mind. London: Saunders, p. 112.

questions.question_text: A 3-year-old boy has a fear of dogs. When he sees a dog around, he experiences marked tachycardia and increased arousal and then he feels an intense feeling of fear. His experience of fear would be best described by which one of the following theories?
questions.explanation:
James–Lange: physiological arousal (tachycardia) occurs first, then the subjective feeling of fear arises from that bodily change.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 53.

questions.question_text: A medical student is puzzled as to why there are so many different subtypes of schizophrenia. She wonders which one of the following terminologies best describes a form of schizophrenia that is characterized by the development of prominent negative symptoms, without much positive symptoms.
questions.explanation:
Simple schizophrenia: insidious onset with predominantly negative symptoms (social withdrawal, apathy) with few or no positive symptoms.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 355.

questions.question_text: The core trainee on examination of a patient noticed that the patient has been having difficulties with performing movements involving that of the face, lips, tongue and cheek. The patient is not able to pretend to blow out a match. What specific type of apraxia is this?
questions.explanation:
This is an example of orobuccal apraxia. The patient has difficulty performing learned, skilled movements of the face, lips, tongue, and cheek on command.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 109.

questions.question_text: When a 2-year-old child is separated from his mother, it will lead to all of the following emotions except
questions.explanation:
Separation in a young child leads first to protest (crying, searching), then despair (apathy, misery), and finally detachment. Anger is not a typical stage.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 64.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not included under ‘Mental Retardation’ International Classification of Diseases (ICD) classification system?
questions.explanation:
ICD-10 includes F70–F73 (mild, moderate, severe, profound), F78 (other mental retardation) and F79 (unspecified). ‘Mental retardation not otherwise specified’ is not a formal ICD-10 category.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 19.

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms is not a part of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM)-IV-TR diagnostic criteria for melancholia?

options.text: Depression regularly worse in the evening

correct_answer.text: Depression regularly worse in the evening

correct_answers.text: Depression regularly worse in the evening

questions.explanation:
In melancholia, depression is typically worse in the morning, not the evening.
Reference: American Psychiatric Association (2000). DSM-IV-TR Diagnostic Criteria. Washington, DC.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman presents with anxiety. You order a thyroid function test. Her serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level is 0.3 mU/L (normal range: 0.5–5 mU/L) and her total thyroxine is 90 mmol/L (normal range: 70–140 mmol/L). The patient does not have a non-thyroidal illness and is not on drug treatment that could suppress TSH. Physical examination shows no goitre. What is your next step?

options.text: Check serum free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3)

correct_answer.text: Check serum free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3)

correct_answers.text: Check serum free thyroxine (FT4) and free triiodothyronine (FT3)

questions.explanation:
With low TSH and normal total T4, measure free T4 and T3 to exclude overt hyperthyroidism before further investigations.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 575–576.

questions.question_text: In order to make the diagnosis of post-schizophrenia depression, the schizophrenic illness must have occurred within which of the following duration of time?
questions.explanation:
Post-schizophrenic depression is diagnosed when depressive symptoms emerge within 12 months of a schizophrenic episode.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 355.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman complained of depression and her GP started her on citalopram. After 2 weeks of treatment, she complains of lethargy, muscle weakness and nausea. The GP wants to know the most likely cause for her symptoms. Your answer is
questions.explanation:
SSRIs often cause hyponatraemia in the elderly, presenting with lethargy, muscle weakness, and nausea.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 1110–1112.

questions.question_text: You have been asked to interview a prisoner, as the prison officers have noticed abnormalities in his behaviour. It was noted that he would not eat his food unless they were packaged, and at times, he attempted to cover his head with his clothes. When the officers asked him the reasons for doing so, he told them he needed to do so as he believed that there were people around who could get to know what he was thinking. What psychopathology does this represent?
questions.explanation:
Thought broadcasting is the delusion that one’s thoughts are being broadcast aloud so others can hear them.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 7.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man is recently diagnosed with Huntington’s disease. He is very concerned about the diagnosis. He has read information from the Internet about Huntington’s disease. Which of the following statements is false?

options.text: Patients with Huntington’s disease may suffer from akinetic mutism at late stage
Patients with Huntington’s disease have a higher risk of committing suicide compared to the general population
Patients with Huntington’s disease will die in 5–10 years after the onset of visible symptoms
Most patients with Huntington’s disease die of pneumonia
The longer length of trinucleotide repeats is associated with faster progression of symptoms

correct_answer.text: Patients with Huntington’s disease will die in 5–10 years after the onset of visible symptoms

correct_answers.text: Patients with Huntington’s disease will die in 5–10 years after the onset of visible symptoms

questions.explanation:
Survival after visible symptom onset is typically 15–20 years, not 5–10 years.
Reference: Walker FO (2007). Huntington’s disease. Lancet, 369: 219.

questions.question_text: The core trainee was administering the Mini Mental State Examination for one of the patients. It was noted that the patient was unable to draw the interconnected double pentagon. What form of apraxia is this?
questions.explanation:
Constructional apraxia involves difficulty reproducing simple geometric patterns and connecting parts together, often from nondominant parietal lesions.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 108.

questions.question_text: An 11-month-old baby is shown his favourite toy. His mother then covers the toy with a cloth. The baby reaches out to remove the cloth and grasps the toy. According to Piaget, which concept best describes the aforementioned phenomenon?
questions.explanation:
Object permanence is the understanding that objects continue to exist even when out of sight.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 113–115.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man is referred by his GP for depression after the death of his father. Based on the DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criteria, which of the following symptoms favours the diagnosis of bereavement rather than major depressive disorder?

options.text: Auditory hallucination of hearing voices from his father
Guilt about delay in sending his father to the hospital
Thought of dying with his father

questions.explanation:
Based on the DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criteria, the presence of the
following symptoms would suggest major depressive episode:
1.  Guilt about things other than actions taken or not taken by the survivor at the
time of the death
2.  thought of death other than the survivor feeling that he or she would be better
off dead or should have died with the deceased person
3.  Morbid preoccupation with worthlessness
4.  Marked psychomotor retardation
5.  Prolonged and marked functional impairment
6.  Hallucinatory experiences other than thinking that he or she hears the voice of,
or transiently sees the image of, the deceased person.

questions.question_text: Based on Parsons’s model, the role of doctors includes all of the following, with the exception of
questions.explanation:
Parsons’ sick-role model includes defining, legitimizing, diagnosing, and offering help, but not imposing costs.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 119.

questions.question_text: The Camberwell Family Interview has been used to assess expressed emotions. Which combination of factors has been identified to be predictive of relapse?
questions.explanation:
High expressed emotion (critical comments, hostility, emotional over-involvement) predicts relapse.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 121.

questions.question_text: Based on the Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Scale, which of the following is associated with the highest life change value?
questions.explanation:
Marital separation scores 65 life change units, the highest of listed events.
Reference: Holmes TH, Rahe RH (1967). The Social Readjustment Rating Scale. Journal of Psychosomatic Research, 11: 213–218.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements accurately reflect the similarities between depression in the young and depression in the old, with the exception of

options.text: Sleep disturbances (such as early morning awakening, subjective poor sleep quality)

questions.explanation:
Depressive pseudodementia—prominent cognitive impairment—is more common in late-life depression.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 710.

questions.question_text: A junior doctor is having her first night call. She sees a man walking alone in the hospital corridor at 3:00 am. Based on her experience, there should be staff working in the hospital in the middle of the night. She deduced this man is either a medical or nursing staff. Which of the following types of processing is she most likely using in her deduction?
questions.explanation:
Top-down processing uses prior knowledge and expectations to interpret sensory information.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 229, 238.

questions.question_text: A core trainee was asked to review a newly admitted patient prior to the ward rounds. During physical examination, he noted that on attempting to move the patient’s arm upwards, it stays in the same position thereafter. He is unable to ask the patient to relax his arm and this lasted for a total duration of 2 hours. This sign is commonly referred to as
questions.explanation:
Waxy flexibility is the ‘plastic’ resistance where a limb remains in the position it is placed.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 3.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man drinks alcohol every morning before going to the office and he is often late to work due to slowness. He drinks again during lunchtime. After coming home, he usually needs to drink at least 8 units of alcohol before he sleeps because he has repeated thoughts that alcohol calms his nerves. His drinking habit has been the same for the past 5 years. A medical student wants to describe his behaviour. Which of the following description is incorrect?

options.text: Lack of resistance to control drinking
Rationalization of the need to drink
Tolerance to the effects of alcohol

questions.explanation:
‘Obsession’ is a DSM term for intrusive thoughts; here it is better described as ‘preoccupation’ not true obsession.
Reference: World Health Organization (1994). ICD-10 Classification of Mental and Behavioural Disorders. Geneva.

questions.question_text: The following are signs and symptoms indicative of an insult to the dominant parietal lobe, with the exception of
questions.explanation:
Asomatognosia (lack of awareness of one’s body parts) occurs with nondominant parietal lesions.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 114.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man is referred by his GP for depression after the death of his father. He exhibits almost all symptoms of depression except worthlessness and active suicidal ideation. Based on the DSM-IV-TR criteria, what is the maximum duration of symptoms to meet the diagnostic criteria of uncomplicated bereavement rather than major depression?
questions.explanation:
In DSM-IV-TR, the category of uncomplicated bereavement is
designated for virtually all symptoms of depression experienced during the rst 2
months aer the loss, with the exception of extreme feelings of worthlessness or active
suicidal ideation. If the duration is longer than 2 months, the patient is considered to
suffer from major depression and warrants antidepressant treatment

questions.question_text: A widely used toolkit for further research into life events and associated psychiatric disorder would be the Life Events and Difficulties Schedule (LEDS) proposed by Brown and Harries (1978). All of the following statements regarding LEDS are true, with the exception of

options.text: It is based on a semi-structured interview
40 areas are being probed during the interview
Detailed narratives are obtained regarding events, including their circumstances
It has a high level of reliability
It has a high level of validity

correct_answer.text: 40 areas are being probed during the interview

correct_answers.text: 40 areas are being probed during the interview

questions.explanation:
LEDS probes 38 areas, not 40. It is semi-structured, elicits detailed narratives, and has high reliability and validity.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 122.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following toolkits would be most useful for evaluating damage to the brain?

options.text: Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status

questions.explanation:
The Halstead–Reitan Battery is a comprehensive neuropsychological test battery for assessing brain damage and lateralization.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 92.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Piaget’s cognitive development theory is correct?

options.text: In the preoperational stage, rules are believed to be inviolable
The preoperational stage is linked to circular reactions
Piaget held that conservation was established in the preoperational stage
Object permanence gets fully developed during the preoperational stage
The preoperational stage is linked to conservation of fluid volume

correct_answer.text: In the preoperational stage, rules are believed to be inviolable

correct_answers.text: In the preoperational stage, rules are believed to be inviolable

questions.explanation:
In the preoperational stage (age 2–7), children view rules as unchangeable ‘authority morality.’
Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD (2002). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: Arnold, pp. 70–71.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman finds it difficult to not drink at all throughout pregnancy. She is currently 10 weeks pregnant. She wants to know the upper limits of units of alcohol she can take per week. Your answer is
questions.explanation:
Current guidelines permit up to 1–2 units, once or twice weekly (≈1–4 units/week) as not shown to harm the fetus.
Reference: RCOG Statement 5 (1999): Alcohol Consumption and the Outcomes of Pregnancy.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old female is here to seek help from the CAMHS psychiatrist. She shared that her son James has been too much for her to handle. He not only skips school for no reason, but has been getting himself into bad company and has been recently using drugs too. What diagnosis do you think the CAMHS consultant would label James with?
questions.explanation:
Conduct disorder involves a repetitive pattern violating rights of others or societal norms, lasting ≥6 weeks.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 637.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants exhibit alpha-receptor antagonism and serotonin receptor inhibition?
questions.explanation:
Mirtazapine is a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antagonist (NaSSA), blocking α2-adrenergic and 5-HT2 receptors.
Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 426, 907.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male has been referred by his GP to the mental health service. Over the past 3 months or so, he has been feeling increasingly troubled by his neighbours. He believes that they are deliberately sending in radiation to harm him and his mother. In addition, he claims that he is able to hear his neighbours making demeaning remarks by the wall. At times, he is even more troubled as they seemed to be commenting on his every action. What form of psychopathology does he present with?
questions.explanation:
He reports voices commenting on his behavior—running commentary, a form of third-person auditory hallucination.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 7.

questions.question_text: A junior doctor is having her first night call. She sees a man walking alone in the hospital corridor at 3:00 am. He wears a white coat and holds a stethoscope. She deduces that he must be a medical doctor. Which of the following types of processing is she most likely using in her deduction?
questions.explanation:
In bottom-up (data-driven) perceptual processing, perception is a direct
process and determined by the information presented to the sensory receptors of the
observer. In suboptimal viewing condition, raw sensory information is analysed into
basic features such as colour or movement. these features are then recombined at
higher brain centres, where they are compared to stored images.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old male has been seen by the addiction services and he has since been abstinent from alcohol for the past 3 months. However, he is still bothered by recurrent auditory hallucinations. Which of the following is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Alcoholic hallucinosis features persistent auditory hallucinations in a clear sensorium among heavy drinkers or recent abstainers, without the autonomic disturbance of delirium tremens.
Reference: Puri BK, Hall A, Ho R (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. London: CRC Press, p. 518.

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old man is referred by his GP for depression, memory impairment, dgety hands and ycatcher’s tongue. His father committed suicide at the age of 47. His grandfather suffered from behavioural problems and died at the age of 50. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This man presents with chorea, and the most likely diagnosis is Huntington’s disease in this age group supported by family history. Option (e) is possible but unlikely to start at this age. Option (a) causes neuropathy or myelopathy. Option (c) causes back and leg pain.

questions.question_text: Which stage of Kohlberg theory of moral development is achieved at the conventional stage?
questions.explanation: According to Kohlberg, at the pre-conventional level, morality is externally controlled by punishment and rewards. At the conventional level, societal laws cannot be disobeyed as they ensure societal order (i.e. social-order-maintaining orientation) and interpersonal cooperation (i.e. good-boy/good-girl orientation). At the post-conventional level, morality is defined in terms of abstract principles (i.e. social-contract and universal ethical principle orientations).

questions.question_text: A 21-year-old female medical student was brought in by the university counsellor as she was in shock and anger after being informed that she had failed in all subjects in her examinations and that she would need to repeat the first year. When you examined her, she was in a daze with purposeless overactivity. The counsellor would like to know when her symptoms would start to disappear. Based on the ICD-10 criteria, the answer is
questions.explanation: Based on the ICD-10 criteria for acute stress disorder. For transient stress which can be relieved, the symptoms begin to diminish after 8 hours.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old university student has decided that he needs to see a psychiatrist as he has a fear of darkness since youth. However, he tells the psychiatrist that he is not overtly distressed when he is in the dark and he does not take measures to avoid being in darkness. Which one of the following statements is true?

options.text: He has a specific phobia, as the fear of darkness is out of proportion to the norm.
He has a specific phobia, as the fear of darkness cannot be reasoned or explained away.
He has a specific phobia, as the feelings of fear are way beyond his own voluntary control.
He has no specific phobia, as the fear of darkness is not included in the list of specific phobia.
He does not have specific phobia, as there is no avoidance behaviour in his case.

correct_answer.text: He does not have specific phobia, as there is no avoidance behaviour in his case.

correct_answers.text: He does not have specific phobia, as there is no avoidance behaviour in his case.

questions.explanation: In this clinical situation, he does not have a specific phobia, as in order for the diagnosis to be made, the fear he experienced needs to be out of proportion to the norm, and cannot be reasons or explained away, and be beyond voluntary control and must have led to avoidance.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman suffers from bipolar disorder and she has been treated with lithium. She is concerned about renal and thyroid dysfunction. She wants to change the mood stabilizer. Which of the following medications has the least prophylactic effect against future manic episodes?
questions.explanation: Topiramate has the least prophylactic effects against future manic episodes.

questions.question_text: A medical student is puzzled and confused about the signs and symptoms associated with mania and hypomania. Which of the following is not one of the classical signs and symptoms of someone with a diagnosis of mania?

options.text: Marked irritability, out of keeping with character

questions.explanation: All of the aforementioned are classical clinical signs and symptoms of mania, with the exception of memory impairment. The core symptoms for mania include increased self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, being more talkative than usual, having flights of ideas, being easily distracted and having an increase in goal-directed activity or psychomotor agitation. There might also be excessive involvement in activities that have a high potential for painful and sexual consequences.

questions.question_text: Which of the following metabolic causes is least likely to cause chorea?
questions.explanation: Hypercalacaemia causes constipation, bone pain, nephrolithiasis and psychiatric symptoms. On the other hand, hypocalacaemia causes Trousseau sign (inflating the blood pressure cuff and maintaining the cuff pressure above systolic will cause carpal spasms) and Chvostek’s sign (tapping of the inferior portion of the zygoma will produce facial spasms). Options (b) to (e) can present acutely with movement disorder and confusion.

questions.question_text: Nondominant temporal lobe damage could potentially lead to impaired performance on this particular test:
questions.explanation: The Rey–Osterrieth Test would be capable of picking up these deficits. In this visual memory test, the subject is presented with a complex design. The subject is asked to copy the design, and then, 40 minutes later, without previous notification that this will occur, the subject is asked to draw the same design again from memory. Nondominant temporal lobe damage could lead to impaired performance on this test, whereas dominant temporal lobe damage tends not to (but is associated with verbal memory difficulties).

questions.question_text: With regards to the aetiology of schizophrenia, which of the following statements is true about the risk of developing schizophrenia among immigrants?

options.text: Social factors are less in importance in predisposing individuals towards schizophrenia as compared to biological factors.
Afro-Caribbean immigrants to the United Kingdom have a higher risk of schizophrenia.
Afro-Caribbean immigrants have the same risk as the population in their native countries.
First-generation immigrants are more likely to develop schizophrenia and hence efforts should be focused on them.
The higher rates of schizophrenia in urban areas is mainly due to migration.

correct_answer.text: Afro-Caribbean immigrants to the United Kingdom have a higher risk of schizophrenia.

correct_answers.text: Afro-Caribbean immigrants to the United Kingdom have a higher risk of schizophrenia.

questions.explanation: The option (b) is true. This phenomenon is seen in the second generation of immigrants. The higher prevalence of schizophrenia in urban areas is a result of the interaction of genetic factors, migration, higher rates of social deprivation and social problems in the inner city.

questions.question_text: A mother is worried that her child will develop bipolar disorder. Which of the following genes has been found to be associated with an increased risk of developing bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation: This gene has been implicated in the aetiology of predisposing individuals towards bipolar disorders.

questions.question_text: This is a psychiatric disorder that is characterized by the following cluster of symptoms: cataplexy and excessive daytime sleepiness. The most likely clinical diagnosis would be
questions.explanation: The core symptom would be excessive daytime sleepiness. There would also be other symptoms such as hypersomnia, sleep attacks, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations and sleep paralysis.

questions.question_text: Which particular subtypes of schizophrenia has been believed to have an increased rate of suicide?
questions.explanation: Post-schizophrenia depression has been associated with an increased risk of suicide. Post-schizophrenic depression is diagnosed when there is prolonged depressive symptom when the psychotic symptoms have subsided and depression then occurs within 12 months of the schizophrenic episode.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman suffers from depression and she is very concerned about gastrointestinal side effects. Which of the following antidepressants causes the most intense gastrointestinal side effects?
questions.explanation: Sertraline causes most intense gastrointestinal side effects.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about emotion is true?

options.text: According to the James–Lange theory, emotions have primacy over physiology.
According to the Cannon–Bard theory, the emotion-arousing stimulus is processed by the hypothalamus.
According to Lazarus, emotions can be without cognition.
Facial expression can affect emotional response.

correct_answer.text: Facial expression can affect emotional response.

correct_answers.text: Facial expression can affect emotional response.

questions.explanation: Option (e) is true. Laird tested the facial feedback hypothesis in his study on the effects of facial expression on the quality of emotional experience. It was found that participants rated cartoon slides as funnier when they had a ‘smiling’ expression than while they were ‘frowning’. They also described feeling angrier when ‘frowning’ and happier when ‘smiling’.

questions.question_text: A patient who has a long-standing history of schizophrenia has been on continuous follow-up with the community psychiatric nurse. He has been concordant to treatment. However, lately he vocalizes that some of his symptoms seem to be coming back. He is complaining of having difficulties in thinking as he believes that every black car that passes by his house has an electronic device within to jam up his thoughts. What form of psychopathology is this?
questions.explanation: Delusional perception refers to the delusional theme that events, objects or other people in one’s immediate environment have a particular and unusual significance.

questions.question_text: The triad of narcolepsy is classically defined as

options.text: Daytime sleep attacks, catalepsy, hypnogogic hallucination
Daytime sleep attacks, catalepsy, hypnopompic hallucination
Daytime sleep attacks, cataplexy, hypnogogic hallucination
Daytime sleep attacks, cataplexy, hypnopompic hallucination
Night-time sleep attacks, cataplexy, hypnopompic hallucination

correct_answer.text: Daytime sleep attacks, cataplexy, hypnogogic hallucination

correct_answers.text: Daytime sleep attacks, cataplexy, hypnogogic hallucination

questions.explanation: Narcolepsy refers to the daytime sleep attacks without warning. Cataplexy are episodes of partial (often face or jaw) or complete loss of muscle tone that result in the patient falling to the ground. Hypnogogic hallucinations are pre-sleep dreams associated with sleep-onset REM activity.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding diagnostic criteria for panic disorder is false?

options.text: Based on the DSM-IV-TR, panic disorder is classified into panic disorder with agoraphobia and panic disorder without agoraphobia.
Based on the DSM-IV-TR, agoraphobia is classified into agoraphobia without history of panic disorder and panic disorder with agoraphobia.
Based on the ICD-10, agoraphobia is classified into agoraphobia without history of panic disorder and panic disorder with agoraphobia.
Based on the ICD-10, panic disorder is classified into panic disorder with agoraphobia and panic disorder without agoraphobia.
Based on the ICD-10 criteria further define severe panic disorder of having at least 4 panic attacks per week over a 4-week period.

correct_answer.text: Based on the ICD-10, panic disorder is classified into panic disorder with agoraphobia and panic disorder without agoraphobia.

correct_answers.text: Based on the ICD-10, panic disorder is classified into panic disorder with agoraphobia and panic disorder without agoraphobia.

questions.explanation: Only the DSM-IV-TR but not the ICD-10 classifies panic disorder into panic disorder with agoraphobia and panic disorder without agoraphobia.

questions.question_text: The following statements about the Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) are true, with the exception of

options.text: It is a relatively brief test that could be routinely used to rapidly detect possible underlying dementia.
It could help to estimate the relative degree of severity of dementia.
It could help to follow up on dementia and progression over a period of time.
It cannot be used to differentiate between dementia and delirium.
It includes tests of short-term memory and immediate recall memory.

correct_answer.text: It cannot be used to differentiate between dementia and delirium.

correct_answers.text: It cannot be used to differentiate between dementia and delirium.

questions.explanation: The MMSE could help to differentiate between dementia and delirium. The MMSE is a brief test that can be routinely used to rapidly detect possible dementia, to estimate the severity of cognitive impairment and to follow the course of cognitive changes over time.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following dementia rating scales could be given to caregivers for an assessment of the cognitive functions of an individual?
questions.explanation: The Blessed Dementia Scale is a questionnaire that can be given to a care-giver or relative for administration. There are three sets of questions within the questionnaire: the first set deals with activities of daily living, the second with further activities of daily living and the third set assesses changes in personality, interest and drive.

questions.question_text: There has been much media attention about how dangerous patients with schizophrenia could be. What is the actual estimated risk of violence amongst patients with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: The prevalence of recent aggressive behaviour among outpatients with schizophrenia has been estimated to be around 5%.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man, after brain injury to the nondominant parietal lobe, came to believe that he has seen himself on a number of occasions while travelling to different cities in his country. He is aware of himself both inside and outside his body. He feels that his office has been copied and exists in two different cities. Which of the following statements is false?

options.text: The knowledge of having a double is occasionally a delusion, or hallucination but more commonly is a variant of depersonalization.
This condition can occur in other people without psychiatric illness.
This condition consists of a delusion that a double of a person or place exists somewhere else.
This condition is known as reduplicative paramnesia.
This condition is a perceptual rather than ideational or cognitive disturbance.

correct_answer.text: This condition is a perceptual rather than ideational or cognitive disturbance.

correct_answers.text: This condition is a perceptual rather than ideational or cognitive disturbance.

questions.explanation: This condition is known as reduplicative paramnesia. It is actually an ideational or cognitive disturbance rather than a purely perceptual one.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not one of Cannon’s critiques of the James–Lange theory?

options.text: Emotions can be independent of bodily responses.
Similar visceral changes can accompany different emotions.
Overt behaviour can lead to emotions without visceral changes.
Emotions can occur before somatic responses.

correct_answer.text: Overt behaviour can lead to emotions without visceral changes.

correct_answers.text: Overt behaviour can lead to emotions without visceral changes.

questions.explanation: Two studies by Valins and Laird suggested that overt behaviour could lead to emotions without visceral changes. These studies support the James–Lange theory by showing that behaviour alone can influence emotional experience.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most common type of violence demonstrated by patients with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: Among patients with schizophrenia, the most common type of violence is verbal aggression, with a prevalence of around 45%.

questions.question_text: Restless leg syndrome is most commonly associated with
questions.explanation: Restless leg syndrome is strongly associated with iron deficiency. About one in five patients have low iron stores.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an assessment scale that involves a structured interview with a relative?
questions.explanation: The CAMDEX (Cambridge Examination for Mental Disorders of the Elderly) involves a structured clinical interview with the patient, a structured interview with a relative or informant, and a mini-neuropsychological battery called the CAMCOG.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about Amok is incorrect?

options.text: This is a condition that was initially described in Malays in the mid-sixteenth century.
It occurs only in Malays and there have not been reports of Amok from any other countries.
It consists of a period of withdrawal, followed by a sudden outburst of homicidal aggression in which the sufferer will attack anyone within reach.
The attack usually lasts for several hours until the sufferer is overwhelmed.
Following the attack, the person typically passes into a deep sleep or stupor for several days, and would have subsequent amnesia of the event.

correct_answer.text: It occurs only in Malays and there have not been reports of Amok from any other countries.

correct_answers.text: It occurs only in Malays and there have not been reports of Amok from any other countries.

questions.explanation: Reports of Amok from other countries do exist, thus questioning its position as a culture-bound syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding diagnostic criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder is true?

options.text: The DSM-IV-TR and the ICD-10 specify acute and chronic PTSD.
The DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 specify PTSD with delayed onset.
The DSM-IV-TR specify the minimum duration of disturbance of PTSD is more than 2 months.
If duration of symptoms is less than 4 months, it will be specified as acute PTSD.
The ICD-10, but not the DSM-IV-TR, specify acute and chronic PTSD.

correct_answer.text: The DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 specify PTSD with delayed onset.

correct_answers.text: The DSM-IV-TR and ICD-10 specify PTSD with delayed onset.

questions.explanation: Both the DSM-IV-TR and the ICD-10 specify PTSD with delayed onset if symptoms begin at least six months after the stressor.

questions.question_text: You are a core trainee who has just started out your inpatient psychiatry posting. The consultant asked you to review a patient prior to the ward rounds. When speaking to the patient, you noticed that the patient appeared to keep repeating whatever word you have just mentioned. The phrase that correctly describes this form of psychopathology is
questions.explanation: Echolalia refers to the automatic imitation by the person of another person’s speech.

questions.question_text: A 26-year-old man was exercising at the neighbourhood park at night. He was sweating profusely, and his heart was palpitating. The lights were out at one section of the park, and he became aware of how dark and quiet the surroundings were. The awareness of his surroundings made him feel scared. Which of the following theories best describes the aforementioned phenomenon?
questions.explanation: According to the Schachter–Singer theory, the experience of emotion is a function of physiological arousal and the cognitive appraisal of that arousal in light of situational cues.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman attempts suicide after ingesting 25 50-mg tablets of amitriptyline prescribed by her GP. The patient looks alert. The Accident and Emergency Department consultant asks you to admit this patient to the psychiatric ward, as he thinks that the psychiatric risk is higher than the medical risk. You are concerned about her medical condition. Which part of the ECG would be most significant in assessing her cardiac risk?
questions.explanation: Amitriptyline overdose is associated with QRS prolongation. The length of the QRS interval is most predictive of arrhythmic risk.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of forgetfulness and urinary incontinence. Physical examination shows gait disturbance. Which of the following conditions is the most likely?
questions.explanation: The triad of normal-pressure hydrocephalus is classically defined as memory loss, urinary incontinence and gait disturbance.

questions.question_text: In clinical practice, it is often difficult to differentiate obsession from delusion. Which of the following strongly indicates that a patient suffers from obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) rather than delusional disorder?

options.text: No other psychotic phenomenon such as hallucinations.
The thought content is less bizarre.
The patient believes that the origin of thoughts is from his or her own mind.
The patient tries to resist his thoughts.

correct_answer.text: The patient tries to resist his thoughts.

correct_answers.text: The patient tries to resist his thoughts.

questions.explanation: Resistance to the intrusive thoughts is characteristic of OCD and is not seen in delusional disorder.

questions.question_text: A 44-year-old man suffers from depression. He had severe aortic regurgitation, and aortic valve replacement was performed after percutaneous coronary intervention. He takes warfarin 2 mg every morning. The prothrombin time (PT) is 24.5 seconds (normal range: 12.0–14.5 seconds) and the international normalized ratio (INR) is 3.60 (normal range: 2.50–3.50). Based on the National Institute of Clinical Excellence (NICE) guidelines, which of the following antidepressants would you recommend?
questions.explanation: According to NICE guidelines, mirtazapine should be the antidepressant of choice for patients on warfarin due to minimal interaction.

questions.question_text: In Alzheimer’s disease, the most common EEG pattern is

options.text: Loss of alpha activity and decrease in diffuse slow waves
Loss of alpha activity and increase in diffuse slow waves
Loss of delta activity and decrease in diffuse slow waves
Loss of delta activity and increase in diffuse slow waves
Loss of theta activity and decrease in fast activity

correct_answer.text: Loss of alpha activity and increase in diffuse slow waves

correct_answers.text: Loss of alpha activity and increase in diffuse slow waves

questions.explanation: In Alzheimer’s disease there is loss of posterior alpha activity and an increase in diffuse slow (theta and delta) waves.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements about the culture-bound condition ‘Dhat’ is incorrect?

options.text: It is most prevalent in Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
This is a condition that strictly affects individuals of the Indian culture.
Individuals usually attribute the passage of semen as a consequence of excessive indulgence in masturbation or intercourse.

correct_answer.text: This is a condition that strictly affects individuals of the Indian culture.

correct_answers.text: This is a condition that strictly affects individuals of the Indian culture.

questions.explanation: Although Dhat is most prevalent in South Asia, it has also been reported in other cultures; it is not strictly limited to Indian culture.

questions.question_text: A recent immigrant from Inuit suddenly presents with a marked change of behaviour in public. From the information obtained, she went wild for no reason and started to roll around shouting obscenities. She is now referred to the psychiatrist for assessment. The culture-bound syndrome that the patient is likely to have is
questions.explanation: Piblotoq (Arctic hysteria) is seen among Inuit populations, characterized by sudden outbursts, aggressive behaviour, and subsequent exhaustion or stupor.

questions.question_text: A 44-year-old man suffers from depression. He has a history of myocardial infarction and takes aspirin 100 mg every morning. Based on the NICE guidelines, which of the following antidepressants would you recommend?
questions.explanation: According to NICE guidelines, sertraline is preferred in patients on aspirin due to lower bleeding risk.

questions.question_text: A callus on a tree resembled a monkey, and villagers flocked to the tree to pay homage to the ‘Monkey God’. Which of the following statements about the aforementioned phenomenon is true?

options.text: This phenomenon appears in villagers’ vision after the exposure to the tree has ceased.
This phenomenon is a form of pseudo-hallucination.
This phenomenon is increased by attention.
This phenomenon is associated with delusion shared by villagers.
This phenomenon occurs the first time villagers look at the tree and does not persist.

correct_answer.text: This phenomenon is increased by attention.

correct_answers.text: This phenomenon is increased by attention.

questions.explanation: This is a pareidolic illusion, in which ambiguous stimuli are perceived as meaningful and the effect is increased by attention to the stimulus.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman has informed the psychologist that she is not coming for the psychotherapy session and intends to leave the world. The psychologist gives you a call and you have decided to contact the patient. Her colleagues mention that she has just swallowed a large amount of medication in the office and she is sent to the hospital. Later, you are informed that this patient is admitted to the Accident and Emergency Department. On admission, her arterial blood gas result is as follows: pH = 7.0 (normal: 7.35–7.45), HCO3 = 20 (normal: 22–26) and CO2 >40 (normal: 35–45). Her QTc interval is 600 ms. The consultant from the intensive care unit wants to consult you because they want to know which of the following agents is most likely to contribute to her clinical picture. Your answer is
questions.explanation: This patient presents with metabolic acidosis and QTc prolongation, a picture classically related to tricyclic antidepressant overdose (imipramine).

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man with a history of depression complains of vertigo and tinnitus. The tinnitus has worsened his depression. Which of the following condition is the most likely?
questions.explanation: A history of episodic vertigo with tinnitus and hearing loss points towards Meniere’s disease.

questions.question_text: A patient has requested to have a word with her psychiatrist regarding the therapy session that she has been undergoing. She has undergone four sessions and decided that she needs to stop the sessions. She claims that she is not comfortable with the therapist and finds the therapist to be harsh and critical, much like what her parents used to be like. Which one of the following best explains her negative experiences?
questions.explanation: Transference is when the patient unconsciously projects feelings and attitudes from earlier relationships onto the therapist.

questions.question_text: In terms of prevention of genetic conditions such as Down’s syndrome, genetic screening at what number of weeks would show the presence of raised human chorionic gonadotropin, lowered alpha-fetoprotein and lowered unconjugated estriol?
questions.explanation: These maternal serum markers are screened at around 16 weeks of gestation.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is true with regards to the risk of inheriting bipolar disorder amongst first-degree relatives of patients with bipolar disorder?
questions.explanation: Family studies indicate a 15%–20% increased risk of bipolar disorder among first-degree relatives.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not one of the phases of psychosexual development proposed by Freud?
questions.explanation: Freud’s stages are oral, anal, phallic, latency and genital. There is no 'stagnant' phase.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old mother has been very concerned about Tom, her 4-year-old son. He has developmental delays and poor communication skills. He is unable to reciprocate and interact with others and occasionally does have stereotype mannerisms. Which of the following would be the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The DSM-5 criteria for autistic disorder require persistent deficits in social communication/interaction and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour.

questions.question_text: Elective mutism usually occurs amongst which of the following age groups?
questions.explanation: Selective (elective) mutism most commonly begins around 5–6 years of age.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female is at a welcoming cocktail party for new psychiatric trainees. While she is talking to a consultant, she suddenly hears that someone calls her name. Which of the following attention allows Lucy to recognize her name is called?
questions.explanation: Focused (selective) attention is the ability to attend to one type of information while ignoring other distractions (e.g., hearing one’s name in a crowd).

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding alcoholic hallucinosis is false?

options.text: Auditory hallucinations are more common than visual hallucinations.
The hallucinations may be fragmentary in the beginning.
The hallucinations can lead to persecutory delusions.
The hallucinations respond favourably to antipsychotics.

correct_answer.text: The hallucinations respond favourably to antipsychotics.

correct_answers.text: The hallucinations respond favourably to antipsychotics.

questions.explanation: Alcoholic hallucinosis typically responds poorly to antipsychotics.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man informs you that he took an antidepressant from a GP and developed priapism. Which of the following antidepressants is most likely to be associated with the aforementioned phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Trazodone is known to cause priapism, especially at higher doses.

questions.question_text: A teacher has requested Tom’s parents to bring him to the CAMHS service. He has been extremely difficult and disruptive in class. He does not wait for his turns, is impulsive and is always on the go. He is also not performing well in his school work, as he is not able to concentrate well. Which one of the following would be the most likely clinical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Hyperkinetic disorder (ADHD) is characterized by inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity present across settings and impairing function.

questions.question_text: Based on Freud’s psychosexual developmental theory, which is the phase during which the sex drive remains relatively stable and latent?
questions.explanation: The sexual drive remains relatively latent during the latency stage, which occurs roughly from age 5–6 to puberty.

questions.question_text: A core trainee was asked during his weekly tutorial about the differences between ICD-10 and DSM-5 in the classification of personality disorder. Which one of the following personality disorders could be found on the DSM-5 and not on the ICD-10?
questions.explanation: All of the above except narcissistic personality disorder appear in both ICD-10 and DSM-5; narcissistic PD appears only in DSM-5.

questions.question_text: Based on the Holmes and Rahe Social Readjustment Rating Scale, which one of the following events has been considered to be the most stressful, which may precipitate a psychiatric illness?

options.text: Death of a close family member

questions.explanation: Death of a close spouse scores 100 life change units, the highest on the Social Readjustment Scale.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old Irish man staying in the countryside of Ireland complains of seeing wide views of huge skyscrapers and great avenues in front of him and he feels like he is suddenly in New York City. He has a history of epilepsy. The lesion is most likely to be found in which of the following neuroanatomical areas?
questions.explanation: Vivid, panoramic visual hallucinations (e.g. wide vistas) are characteristic of temporal lobe epilepsy.

questions.question_text: All of the following are factors that might predispose one to acquire schizophrenia, with the exception of

options.text: High level of expressed emotion within the family
Winter excess of birth in schizophrenics

questions.explanation: Low birth weight (not high) and winter-spring excess of birth are associated with schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Carl Jung founded the psychoanalytic school of analytic psychology. He has proposed five different archetypes. Which one of the following correctly describes “the masculine prototype within each person?”
questions.explanation: The animus is the unconscious masculine aspect in women; the anima is the feminine aspect in men.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about panic attacks is incorrect?

options.text: It usually involves recurrent unpredictable attacks of severe anxiety.
These attacks usually last only for a few minutes only.
There might be a sudden onset of palpitation, chest pain, choking, dizziness, depersonalization, together with a secondary fear of dying, losing control or going mad.
It does not result in subsequent avoidance of similar situations.
It may be followed by persistent fear of another attack.

correct_answer.text: It does not result in subsequent avoidance of similar situations.

correct_answers.text: It does not result in subsequent avoidance of similar situations.

questions.explanation: Panic attacks commonly lead to avoidance of the situation in which they occur.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old woman is referred to old-age psychiatric service. She reports several incidents when she suddenly saw several four-inch-high beings wearing hats parading in front of her. She tried to catch one, but could not. She has no past psychiatric history. Her only medical problem is macular degeneration. The patient is most likely to be suffering from
questions.explanation: Charles Bonnet syndrome causes vivid visual hallucinations in patients with significant visual impairment but otherwise intact cognition.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old woman seeks outpatient treatment for her binge eating and self-induced vomiting. Which of the following antidepressants is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in bulimia nervosa.

questions.question_text: The following are aetiological factors that might predispose a child to have conduct disorder, with the exception of

options.text: Conduct disorder is associated with the inheritance of antisocial traits from parents who have demonstrated criminal activities.
Biological factors include the presence of elevated plasma dopamine levels.
Psychological factors include the difficult temperament and a poor fit between temperament and emotional needs.
There has been an association with parental criminality.
There has been an association with repeated physical and sexual abuse.

correct_answer.text: Biological factors include the presence of elevated plasma dopamine levels.

correct_answers.text: Biological factors include the presence of elevated plasma dopamine levels.

questions.explanation:
Biological factors in conduct disorder include low, not elevated, dopamine levels.It is true that conduct disorder is associated with the
inheritance of antisocial traits from parents who have demonstrated criminal activities.
Previous research has demonstrated an association with parental criminality as well as
with repeated physical and sexual abuse

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman is referred by her lawyer after a road traffic accident which occurred one month ago. Her lawyer wants you to certify that she suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Which of the following clinical features is not a predisposing factor in PTSD?

options.text: Lack of control of the accident

correct_answer.text: Lack of control of the accident

correct_answers.text: Lack of control of the accident

questions.explanation: Lack of control over an accident is not an established predisposing factor for PTSD.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman developed depression 2 weeks after delivery. Which of the following is not a risk factor for her condition?

options.text: Ambivalence towards pregnancy prior to delivery
Lack of support from her husband

questions.explanation: Episiotomy is not an established risk factor for postnatal depression.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.text: Culture has a pathoplastic effect on psychopathology.
Personality is not shaped by culture.
The ethnic-minority patients may not perceive the practice of psychiatry as benign.
The nosological systems employed by psychiatry are largely anglocentric and eurocentric.

correct_answer.text: Personality is not shaped by culture.

correct_answers.text: Personality is not shaped by culture.

questions.explanation: Personality is strongly shaped by cultural values and child-rearing practices.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following comorbidities is known to increase the incidences of mortality amongst women with anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: Alcohol dependence in anorexia nervosa is associated with a higher mortality rate.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old male came for his routine outpatient appointment and tells the psychiatrist that he is no longer keen to continue on his selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) antidepressant, as it has affected the sexual side of his relationship. This is commonly due to the action of SSRI on which of the following receptors?
questions.explanation: Stimulation of 5-HT2A/2C receptors by SSRIs is implicated in sexual dysfunction.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old with a history of mitral valve replacement takes warfarin on a daily basis. Her GP has recently prescribed fluoxetine to treat her depression. The interaction between fluoxetine and warfarin will cause which of the following symptoms?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine inhibits warfarin metabolism, increasing bleeding tendency and bruising.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman complains of seeing herself outside her body. Which of the following statements about this phenomenon is false?

options.text: The double image typically appears as semi-transparent.
The experience rarely lasts longer than a few seconds.
The mean age of onset of this phenomenon is 40.
The most common emotional reactions after seeing her double are sadness and bewilderment.
This phenomenon is more common in women.

correct_answer.text: This phenomenon is more common in women.

correct_answers.text: This phenomenon is more common in women.

questions.explanation: Autoscopy is actually more common in men (male:female ≈ 2:1).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a typical cause of olfactory hallucination?
questions.explanation: Olfactory hallucinations are seen in cocaine intoxication, not withdrawal; migraine and temporal lobe epilepsy also produce them.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man suffering from schizophrenia committed suicide one day after discharge from the psychiatric hospital. He killed himself under the influence of command hallucinations. The hospital sentinel event committee found that the patient was discharged prematurely, psychosis was not fully treated and no proper suicide assessment was conducted. The sentinel event committee concluded that this could be a case of negligence. The following constitutes negligence in this case, except

options.text: Family members did not agree with the premature discharge and their opinions were not sought.

questions.explanation: Munchausen syndrome is a form of factitious disorder in which the patient fabricates symptoms for no apparent external gain.

questions.explanation: Newer agents (gabapentin, topiramate, vigabatrin) commonly cause visual adverse effects; sodium valproate is least likely.

questions.question_text: A core trainee has been asked to perform a suicide risk assessment for a patient who has just been admitted to the emergency department following an overdose on 60 tablets of lamotrigine. questions.explanation: Suggestive probes can bias responses; open questions, reflective listening, summarizing and silence are recommended.

questions.question_text: Dementia praecox was a term coined by

questions.question_text: You are able to assess a 20-year-old man who is aggressive and angry towards the staff at the Accident and Emergency Department. Which of the following measures is least useful?

Inform the patient that restraint or seclusion will be used if necessary.
Inform the patient that physical violence is not acceptable in the hospital setting.
Offer the option of using psychotropic medication to calm the patient.

correct_answer.text: Admit own feelings and inform the patient that the staff are frightened of his aggression and anger.

correct_answers.text: Admit own feelings and inform the patient that the staff are frightened of his aggression and anger.

questions.question_text: Plato and Aristotle were responsible for proposing the virtue theory. Which one of the following statements correctly describes what the theory encompasses?

questions.explanation: Oppositional defiant disorder is characterized by angry/irritable mood and argumentativeness toward authority figures without the severe rule-breaking of conduct disorder.

Sublimation refers to the process that utilizes the force of a sexual

Transition, at times of stress and threat, to moods of expression and

questions.question_text: This is a common defence mechanism seen in paranoid patients.
questions.explanation:
In projection, unacceptable qualities, feelings and thoughts or wishes are
projected onto another person or thing. this is very often seen in paranoid patients.

questions.question_text: This is a common defence mechanism seen in patients with OCD.
questions.explanation:
this refers to an attempt that is made to negate or atone for forbidden
thoughts, affects or memories. this defence mechanism is seen, for example, in the

choice

questions.question_text: This refers to a legal concept and construct and refers to the capacity to act and understand.
questions.explanation:
Competence is a legal concept and refers to the capacity to act and
understand. Competence is determined only by the legal system, such as the
competence to adopt a child.

Security to receive and administer bene ts on the behalf of someone else who is not
able to administer money derived from social security and cannot be used to

Hygric hallucination is a superficial hallucination in which the person
feels the presence of fluid in his or her body.

questions.explanation:
Haptic hallucinations are superficial sensations of touch on or under the
skin.

questions.explanation:
Reduplicative hallucination refers to the sensation of the presence of a
duplication of a certain body part.

questions.question_text: She is terrified and shouts, ‘White Lady, White Lady, Go away.’ She perceives the curtain as a female ghost.
questions.explanation:
Illusion. It is an involuntary false perception in which a transformation
of a real object (i.e. curtain) takes place

questions.question_text: She finds the colour in the ward appears to her to be brighter and more vivid than usual.

Visual hyperaesthesia refers to changes in sensory perception in which
there is an increased intensity of visual stimuli

Dysmegalopsia (also known as the Alice in Wonderland effect); illusory

actual size

Pareidolia refers to the type of intense imagery (i.e. Jesus’ face) that
persists even when the person looks at a real object (callus of a tree) in the external
environment

questions.question_text: She reports that she saw a colourfully dressed clown and children dancing in the ward last night.

Peduncular hallucination is a form of vivid and colourful visual
hallucination
